records.name: Schleswig-Holstein
records.current_summary:
The surviving sources for Schleswig-Holstein are framework-level: the July 2026 prison-placement case (a prisoner whose legal gender had been changed under the federal Self-Determination Act sent to a men's prison) that turned Land placement law into a federal reform fight, and a March 2026 constitutional-law survey of the 2023-26 Land reform wave, whose named statutes belong to other Länder.

No Schleswig-Holstein trans statute, ordinance, enforcement series or event-security finding survives in the record; prison administration is a Land competence and visitor exposure tracks the national position.

sources.claim: NOTE: page content did not load at fetch time (France24 returned an access-denied security page); the underlying 16 July 2026 live-news report covers a German court sending a person convicted of neo-Nazi incitement — whose legal gender had been changed to female under the Self-Determination Act — to a men's prison amid public outcry over women's-prison safety, the case that drove the state-level prison-placement law debate discussed in the accompanying analyses.

Framework analysis (Verfassungsblog, 18 Mar 2026) of Länder trans-prisoner placement under the Self-Determination Act (SBGG, in force 1 Nov 2024): placement tracks the legal gender entry unless state law excludes it; constitutional doubts raised about trans-targeted exception clauses. Framework-level for this Land — the July 2026 placement case and the SBGG mechanics are the operative rules; no Schleswig-Holstein-specific statute on file.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Germany (Wikipedia)
sources.claim: The page records that Schleswig-Holstein, with Hesse, Berlin, Bremen and Saarland, tabled a joint motion in the Bundesrat for a ban on conversion therapy, presented in plenary on 12 April 2019; Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia agreed to the motion, Bavaria expressed potential support with modifications, and the federal ban was approved by the Bundestag on 7 May 2020 with support from all parties except the AfD. Documents the state government's concrete action in the federal conversion-therapy ban campaign in a record where no SH-specific trans statute or ordinance survives.

sources.title: Jens Spahn will Pseudotherapien gegen Homosexualität verbieten
sources.claim: Zeit Online (10 April 2019) reports that parallel to Federal Health Minister Jens Spahn's announced plan to ban conversion therapies, Hesse, Berlin, Bremen, Saarland and Schleswig-Holstein planned to present a joint Bundesrat motion (Entschließungsantrag) for a ban that same week. Fixes Schleswig-Holstein by name as one of the five tabling states in the run-up to the 12 April 2019 Bundesrat plenary presentation recorded by Wikipedia's LGBTQ rights in Germany page.

records.name: Canarias
records.current_summary: This division was covered by the dedicated country dossier, which identified no deviation from the national position material enough to score separately (±0.02); it is therefore assessed at the national score.

sources.claim: State Law 4/2023 of 28 February 2023 (BOE no. 51, 1 March 2023), the 'Law for the real and effective equality of trans people and the guarantee of the rights of LGBTI persons' (the 'Trans Law'), applies uniformly across Spain's autonomous communities, including this one: Title II allows adults to rectify their registered sex marker by simple declaration, with no requirement of prior medical diagnosis or treatment, and provides for corresponding document adaptation. The law further mandates public-policy, workplace, health and education measures, and its transitory provisions govern rectification applications pending at entry into force.

Human Rights Watch (16 February 2023) reports the Spanish Congress of Deputies' passage of the Trans Law: legal gender recognition by self-identification through a simple administrative process, replacing the previous requirements of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment. The same law expands access to assisted reproduction, strengthens sexuality education, bans medically unnecessary normalising surgery on intersex children before consent, enables parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, and prohibits LGBTI discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing; children from age 12 can obtain recognition under conditions, a provision that proved contentious. HRW places the reform within European and international standards against disproportionate requirements for legal gender recognition.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Spain (Wikipedia): Canary Islands — same-sex registry 2003, gender-identity non-discrimination law 2014, gender self-declaration since 2021
sources.claim: The English Wikipedia page 'LGBTQ rights in Spain' covers the Canary Islands specifically in its autonomous-community sections: the community created its same-sex couple registry in 2003; it was among the first to ban employment and other discrimination on gender-identity grounds via Ley 8/2014 of 28 October 2014 (non-discrimination on gender-identity grounds and recognition of trans persons' rights, BOE-A-2014-11995); and it has allowed trans people to self-declare their legal gender since 2021, one of 14 communities doing so before the national Ley Trans of 28 February 2023. The Canary Islands are also listed among the communities banning conversion therapies, and Gran Canaria and Tenerife are named internationally known LGBT tourist destinations. For a trans traveler the region therefore stands under a regional anti-discrimination and self-identification regime layered on the 2023 national law this record already cites.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Spain (Wikipedia): La Rioja — same-sex registry 2010, trans-rights law February 2022, gender self-declaration since 2022
sources.claim: The English Wikipedia page 'LGBTQ rights in Spain' covers La Rioja in its autonomous-community sections: La Rioja created its same-sex couple registry in 2010; in February 2022 it passed a regional trans-rights law (the page cites FELGTB's 'Los derechos trans ya son ley en la Rioja', 18 February 2022), joining the communities that let trans people self-declare their legal gender; and it is listed among the communities banning conversion therapies. The regional law gave trans visitors and residents in La Rioja protective rights from 2022, still standing under (and since layered onto) the national Ley Trans of 28 February 2023 that is this record's existing source.

records.name: País Vasco/Euskadi
records.current_summary: No region-specific law or incident series diverges from the national framework, but the country dossier records a mixed finding for this community: with Navarra it tops the state hate-crime statistics (highest per-capita LGTBI-motivated offence rates in the 2024 Interior report) — a result the dossier attributes to intensive reporting and counting, not to danger: the regional government runs its own LGTBI public-order police and an equality observatory maintaining a comparative legislation database, and no Basque statute rollback exists. Net visitor risk is assessed at approximately the national score, with the high recorded counts read as neutral-to-positive.

sources.title: Historia LGBT en el País Vasco (Spanish Wikipedia)
sources.claim: Spanish Wikipedia's dedicated article on LGBT history in the Basque Country: the Basque Parliament passed a specific law against discrimination on grounds of gender identity and recognising the rights of trans people (the page dates it to 2013) and for the first time incorporated an LGTBI perspective into gender-violence prevention in the Basque education system; earlier institutional markers are the first Basque Pride march in Bilbao in 1978, the legalisation of the activist collective EHGAM in 1983, and the creation of Emakunde, the Basque Women's Institute, in 1988. A 2017 survey by the Basque Youth Observatory reported that 9 in 10 Basque young people favour same-sex marriage and legal change of sex, and the page notes Osakidetza (the Basque health service) provided assisted reproduction regardless of sexual orientation, reaffirming that position in 2013. Region-specific confirmation that the Basque Country runs its own non-discrimination legal instruments and equality institutions (Emakunde) under the national framework — the divergence-vs-framework question this record addresses.

records.name: Comunidad Foral de Navarra
records.current_summary: No region-specific law or incident series diverges from the national framework, but the country dossier records a mixed finding for this community: it is the single highest per-capita LGTBI hate-offence region in the 2024 Interior report — a result the dossier reads as a reporting-institution effect, since Pamplona runs an annual anti-LGTBIphobia observatory whose 2025 report documents rising discourse, and the region polices public order with its own force. Net visitor risk is assessed at approximately the national score, with the high recorded counts read as reporting quality rather than a safety deficit.

sources.title: Diversidad sexual en España (Spanish Wikipedia)
sources.claim: National-framework article whose Navarra-specific substance: the earliest documented executions for same-sex acts in the Iberian peninsula occurred in the Kingdom of Navarra — in 1290 a Muslim man was burned in Arguedas for 'yacer con otros', and in 1345 Juce Abolfaça and Simuel Nahamán, two Jews of Olite, were tortured for confessions and burned before a cortege of 20 after the crime of sodomy. For the modern period the article's references cite Diario de Navarra (12 May 2026) reporting that Navarra planned to create an observatory against LGTBI-phobia. The page gives little modern Navarra statute detail (Ley Foral 8/2017 is not substantively covered), so it serves as historical/framework context for the record's claim that the region stands under the national framework without its own substantive divergence; note the May 2026 footnote says the anti-LGTBIphobia observatory was still at the planning stage, which sits in possible tension with the record's summary reference to a 2025 observatory report.

records.name: Región de Murcia
records.current_summary: Assessed materially in line with the national position. Regional LGTBI or equality legislation is recorded for this region in the national policy inventories, but no region-specific incident, ordinance or enforcement finding was identified in the dedicated country dossier for this region; no sub-national facility, expression or assembly restriction exists anywhere in the country, and the 2023 national trans-equality law's implementation (including its education-facing parts) falls to the regional government. The national victimisation baseline applies here: a 2026 federation report found 44% of LGTBI respondents had experienced a hate-motivated incident.

sources.title: BOE-A-2016-6170 — Ley 8/2016, de 27 de mayo, de igualdad social de lesbianas, gais, bisexuales, transexuales, transgénero e intersexuales, y de políticas públicas contra la discriminación por orientación sexual e identidad de género en la Comunidad Autónoma de la Región de Murcia (BOE)
sources.claim: Official gazette text of the Region of Murcia's own LGTBI-equality statute beneath the national framework, confirming this record's claim that regional LGTBI legislation exists for Murcia. Ley 8/2016 of 27 May 2016 (BOE-A-2016-6170) prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics in public and private activity in the region, and within its scope bars any requirement to prove declared gender identity by psychological or medical report. Article 5 creates the Observatorio regional contra la discriminación por orientación sexual e identidad de género, a participation/consultation body in which LGTBI entities are represented. Title IV sets a sanctioning ladder: minor breaches a warning or fine of up to €3,000; serious breaches €3,001–€20,000 (including degrading remarks or incitement to violence against LGBTI persons or their families in the provision of services); very serious breaches €20,001–€45,000, with accessory penalties such as exclusion from regional public aid for up to one year; multiple discrimination raises the infraction grade.

sources.title: Derechos LGBT en España (Spanish Wikipedia, national framework context)
sources.claim: Framework-context source naming this jurisdiction: the Spanish Wikipedia article on LGBT rights in Spain records that the first wave of autonomous-region LGTBI and trans-equality laws was approved in the 2010s in eight regions, explicitly listing Murcia alongside País Vasco, Andalucía, Galicia, Extremadura, Madrid, Baleares and Aragón — the national-inventory evidence behind this record's claim that regional LGTBI legislation is recorded for this region. It also dates the state framework the visitor stands under here: same-sex marriage legalised on 2 July 2005 (some 4,500 same-sex couples married in the law's first year), the 2007 gender-identity law, and the Ley 4/2023 trans-equality law approved in February 2023 (registered sex change from age 16 without medical reports or hormonal treatment), whose implementation the record notes falls to the regional government. Operative regional instrument: Ley 8/2016 de la Región de Murcia.

records.name: Galicia
records.current_summary:
Spain's Law 4/2023 for the real and effective equality of trans people (official gazette text) vests implementation of its administrative and education-facing provisions in the autonomous communities — this region's government among them. The parallel 2023 gender-recognition reform, letting registry entries change by self-declaration from age 12 without medical diagnosis, drew an international rights organisation to rank the country among autonomy-first jurisdictions.

The surviving record adds no Galician statute, ordinance, enforcement series or incident finding; regional value here is implementation posture under the 2023 framework, not separate restriction or separate protection.

sources.claim: Official gazette text (BOE-A-2023-5366) of State Law 4/2023 of 28 February 2023, the law for the real and effective equality of trans people and the guarantee of LGBTI rights. Title II regulates rectification of the registered sex entry by the person's freely expressed will, depathologizes the procedure (no medical diagnosis or treatment requirement) and removes the former age-majority requirement for requesting it, with corresponding document adaptation; Title III provides protection and reparation against LGBTIphobic discrimination and violence. The law mandates measures across administrative, workplace, health and education fields, with public authorities acting within their competences; the education-facing and administrative provisions are implemented by the autonomous communities, this region's government among them.

Human Rights Watch, 16 February 2023, reporting the Spanish Congress of Deputies' passage of the comprehensive LGBTI law known as the 'Trans Law': legal gender recognition by self-identification through a simple administrative process, replacing the prior requirements of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment aligned to the sought marker. The law strengthens sexuality education, bans medically unnecessary normalising surgery on intersex children before their consent, enables parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples and prohibits LGBTI discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing; children from age 12 may obtain recognition under certain conditions, a provision that provoked political conflict. HRW assesses the reform as upholding European and international standards against abusive, disproportionate requirements for legal gender recognition.

records.name: Extremadura
records.current_summary:
Spain's Law 4/2023 (gazette text) leaves implementation of the national trans-equality and self-declaration provisions to the autonomous communities, including this region's government; the 2023 registry reform won the country placement in an international organisation's autonomy-first grouping. The record adds no Extremadura statute, ordinance, enforcement series or incident finding.

This region stands out in national statistics for the LOWEST per-capita recorded rate of hate offences — and the record's own caveat is that the figure reflects how little is counted rather than demonstrated protection. The low number should not be read as reassurance; exposure otherwise tracks the national framework.
